summary: Specifies how to use the US National Security Agency's Suite B cryptographic algorithms with S/MIME secure email. It obsoletes RFC 5008 and is informational. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: Suite B is a fixed set of cryptographic algorithms chosen by the US National Security Agency. RFC 6318 says which of them an S/MIME mail system should use, at two levels of strength, and spells out the small details needed to make a signature or an encrypted message readable by another implementation. It replaces RFC 5008, which was more restrictive about how the two levels could be combined.

questions: which curves does suite b use
subtitle: Which NSA Suite B algorithms an S/MIME email system uses, and how to plug them into signing and encryption.

tldr.problem: Agencies that wanted to protect email with the algorithms of the US National Security Agency's Suite B needed one document saying exactly which algorithms S/MIME should use and how.
tldr.mechanism: It picks two matching sets of algorithms, one for 128-bit and one for 192-bit minimum security: SHA-256 or SHA-384 with ECDSA for signatures, and ECDH, AES Key Wrap and AES in CBC mode for encryption.
tldr.outcome: The document is Informational and now has Historic status. It obsoletes RFC 5008 and allows more freedom in how the two security levels are combined.

today: RFC 6318 is an Informational document with Historic status. It has not been obsoleted, but the algorithms it names are no longer the ones in current use, and the document itself is best read as a record of how the Suite B requirements were expressed for S/MIME. It obsoletes RFC 5008, which was more restrictive about combining the two security levels, and it points at RFC 5751 for the S/MIME message specification itself and RFC 5652 for the Cryptographic Message Syntax it builds on.

sections.title: Why Suite B for S/MIME
sections.content:
The National Security Agency's fact sheet on Suite B cryptography explains the background. A Cryptographic Interoperability Strategy was developed to increase assured rapid sharing of information within the United States and between it and its partners, using a common suite of public standards, protocols, algorithms and modes called the Secure Sharing Suite. The use of selected public cryptographic standards and Suite B is the core of that strategy. In 2005 the NSA announced Suite B cryptography, which built on the national policy for using the Advanced Encryption Standard to protect national security systems and information. Besides AES, Suite B includes algorithms for key exchanges, digital signatures and hashing, all selected from cryptography approved by NIST for use by the US Government.

RFC 6318 specifies the conventions for using those algorithms in S/MIME as specified in RFC 5751. S/MIME makes use of the Cryptographic Message Syntax, and in particular the signed-data and enveloped-data content types. Only Suite B compliance for S/MIME is addressed; other uses of the Cryptographic Message Syntax are outside its scope.

Most of the Suite B algorithms are used elsewhere as well, so the conventions needed for them are already specified in other documents. This document points at the source of each convention and repeats some of the relevant detail to help developers who choose to support Suite B. It obsoletes RFC 5008, and the memo gives the primary reason: to allow greater flexibility in how the Suite B security levels are used. It also removes some duplication between this document and the RFCs it references.
sections.plainLanguage: Suite B is the NSA's pick of standard algorithms for protecting government traffic. This document says which of them belong in an S/MIME message, and points at the other documents that already describe how each one is used.

sections.title: Two Security Levels, Two Signing Sets and Two Key Sets
sections.content:
Suite B offers two suites of algorithms for key agreement, key derivation, key wrap and content encryption, and two possible combinations of hash and signing algorithm. The algorithms are defined to support two minimum levels of cryptographic security: 128 and 192 bits. For signed messages, Suite B follows the direction set in RFC 5753 and RFC 5754. Sig Set 1 pairs SHA-256 with ECDSA using the P-256 curve; Sig Set 2 pairs SHA-384 with ECDSA using the P-384 curve.

For encrypted messages, Suite B follows the direction set in RFC 5753 and the conventions in RFC 3565. KE Set 1 pairs ECDH with P-256, SHA-256 key derivation, AES-128 Key Wrap and AES-128 CBC content encryption. KE Set 2 pairs ECDH with P-384, SHA-384 key derivation, AES-256 Key Wrap and AES-256 CBC content encryption. The two elliptic curves each appear in the literature under two names: nistp256 is P-256 and secp256r1, and nistp384 is P-384 and secp384r1.

A system configured at a minimum of 128 bits that encrypts must use either KE Set 1 or KE Set 2, with KE Set 1 preferred. A digital signature, if applied, must use either Sig Set 1 or Sig Set 2, independently of the encryption choice, so the algorithm set used for a signed message does not have to match the one used for an encrypted message. A recipient at that level must be able to verify Sig Set 1 signatures and should be able to verify Sig Set 2 signatures. A system configured at a minimum of 192 bits that encrypts must use KE Set 2, a signature must use Sig Set 2, and a recipient must be able to verify Sig Set 2 signatures.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two strength levels, 128 and 192 bits, and for each there is a matching set of algorithms. At the lower level a system may pick either signing set and either encryption set independently; at the higher level everything must come from the stronger set.

sections.title: Message Digests and Digital Signatures
sections.content:
SHA-256 and SHA-384 are the Suite B message digest algorithms. The conventions for using them with the Cryptographic Message Syntax are in RFC 5754, and Suite B implementations must follow them. Within the signed-data content type, digest algorithm identifiers are located in the SignedData digestAlgorithms field and the SignerInfo digestAlgorithm field. For both hashes the AlgorithmIdentifier parameters field is optional, and if it is present it must contain a NULL. Implementations must accept algorithm identifiers with absent parameters and with NULL parameters, and must generate them with absent parameters.

ECDSA is the Suite B digital signature algorithm, and the conventions for it are in RFC 5753. Any public key certificate used to verify an S/MIME signature must comply with the Suite B Certificate Profile in RFC 5759. Within the signed-data content type, signature algorithm identifiers are located in the SignerInfo signatureAlgorithm field of SignedData and in the SignerInfo signatureAlgorithm field of countersignature attributes. The identifiers for ECDSA with SHA-256 and ECDSA with SHA-384 come from RFC 5480, and when either is used the AlgorithmIdentifier parameters field must be absent.

Signing with ECDSA produces two values, usually called r and s. To carry them as one signature they must be encoded using the ECDSA-Sig-Value type from RFC 5480, which is a sequence of the two integers r and s.
sections.plainLanguage: Signing an S/MIME message under Suite B means hashing the content with SHA-256 or SHA-384 and signing that hash with ECDSA on one of two standard curves. The certificates used to check the signature have to follow the Suite B certificate profile.

sections.title: Key Agreement, Key Derivation and Key Wrap
sections.content:
The Cryptographic Message Syntax accommodates several key management techniques: key agreement, key transport, previously distributed symmetric keys and passwords. In Suite B for S/MIME, ephemeral-static key agreement must be used. When a key agreement algorithm is used, a key-encryption algorithm is also needed, and there AES Key Wrap from RFC 3394 must be used. The key-encryption key used with the key wrap is obtained from a key derivation function, and Suite B has two of them, one based on SHA-256 and one based on SHA-384.

ECDH is the Suite B key agreement algorithm. Because S/MIME is store-and-forward, ephemeral-static ECDH is always employed: the message originator has an ephemeral key pair and the recipient has a static key pair whose public key is represented by an X.509 certificate, which must comply with the Suite B Certificate Profile. Within the enveloped-data content type, the key agreement algorithm identifier sits in the EnvelopedData RecipientInfos KeyAgreeRecipientInfo keyEncryptionAlgorithm field. For KE Set 1 that identifier must be the single-pass Diffie-Hellman scheme with the SHA-256 key derivation, and its parameter must name the AES-128 key wrap; for KE Set 2 it must be the single-pass scheme with the SHA-384 key derivation, with the AES-256 key wrap named as the parameter.

The key derivation functions work from the shared secret Z produced by ephemeral-static ECDH. The derivation hashes the concatenation of Z, a counter and a structure called ECC-CMS-SharedInfo, which carries the identifier of the key wrap algorithm, optionally a random value supplied by the originator, and the length in bits of the key to be derived, written as a 32-bit unsigned number. With a 128-bit AES key that length must be 0x00000080, and with a 256-bit key it must be 0x00000100. Leading zero bits of Z must be preserved, Z must be exactly 256 bits for KE Set 1 and exactly 384 bits for KE Set 2, and the counter starts at 1 and is not incremented, because exactly one iteration is needed. The key-encryption key is then the most significant 128 bits of the SHA-256 output for KE Set 1, and the most significant 256 bits of the SHA-384 output for KE Set 2. The memo notes that the only source of secret entropy in this computation is Z, so the effective key space is limited by the size of Z as well as by the security level of the curve, though a different random value per message produces a different key-encryption key each time.
sections.plainLanguage: Encrypting a message needs a key for the content, and that key has to be shared with the recipient. The two sides agree a shared secret with elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman, turn it into a wrapping key with a hash, and use AES Key Wrap to wrap the content key under it. The random value the sender adds makes each message use a different wrapping key.

sections.title: Encrypting the Message Content
sections.content:
AES in Cipher Block Chaining mode is the Suite B content-encryption algorithm, and the conventions for using AES with the Cryptographic Message Syntax are in RFC 3565. With KE Set 1 the content must be encrypted with AES-128 in CBC mode, and with KE Set 2 it must be AES-256 in CBC mode. Within the enveloped-data content type, the content-encryption algorithm identifier is located in the EnvelopedData EncryptedContentInfo contentEncryptionAlgorithm field, and the algorithm is used to encipher the content in the encryptedContent field.

The AlgorithmIdentifier parameters field must be present, and it must contain the initialisation vector, which is an octet string of 16 octets. The 16-octet initialisation vector is generated at random by the originator, and the memo points to RFC 4086 for guidance on generating random values.
sections.plainLanguage: The message body itself is encrypted with AES in CBC mode: 128-bit for the lower Suite B set and 256-bit for the higher one. Each message gets a fresh random 16-octet starting value, sent alongside so the recipient can decrypt.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo says that all of the algorithms and algorithm identifiers in it were specified in previous documents, and that two minimum levels of security may be achieved using this specification. Users must consider their risk environment to decide which level is appropriate for their own use.

For the rest it points at the existing text: RFC 4086 for guidance on generating random values, RFC 5652 for the security considerations of the Cryptographic Message Syntax as a way of signing and encrypting data, RFC 3370 for cryptographic algorithm implementation concerns in that context, RFC 5753 for the use of elliptic curve cryptography in the Cryptographic Message Syntax, and RFC 3565 for the use of AES in it.
sections.plainLanguage: The document adds no new cryptography of its own. It says the choice between the two strength levels is a matter of what is at stake, and points at the documents that already cover how the algorithms should be implemented.

viz.caption: THE FOUR SUITE B ALGORITHM SETS (RFC 6318 SECTION 1.3)

items.title: Sig Set 1
items.text: SHA-256 digest with ECDSA on the P-256 curve.

items.title: Sig Set 2
items.text: SHA-384 digest with ECDSA on the P-384 curve.

items.title: KE Set 1
items.text: ECDH with P-256, SHA-256 key derivation, AES-128 key wrap, AES-128 CBC content encryption.

items.title: KE Set 2
items.text: ECDH with P-384, SHA-384 key derivation, AES-256 key wrap, AES-256 CBC content encryption.

items.label: P-256
items.desc: The NIST curve also known as secp256r1, used by Sig Set 1 and KE Set 1.

items.label: P-384
items.desc: The NIST curve also known as secp384r1, used by Sig Set 2 and KE Set 2.

items.label: AES-128 Key Wrap
items.desc: The key wrap algorithm for KE Set 1.

items.label: AES-256 Key Wrap
items.desc: The key wrap algorithm for KE Set 2.

data.title: Deriving the key-encryption key
data.code:
KM = Hash ( Z || Counter || ECC-CMS-SharedInfo )

KEK = KM ( 1 ) = Hash ( Z || Counter=1 || ECC-CMS-SharedInfo )

KE Set 1: KEK = most significant 128 bits of the SHA-256 output
KE Set 2: KEK = most significant 256 bits of the SHA-384 output
